chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: IL&FS and the 2018 NBFC Liquidity Crunch

body.text: In 2018 India learned that a financial crisis does not need a bank. One infrastructure lender defaulted, and within weeks the entire shadow banking system was struggling to borrow. The IL&FS episode is the clearest Indian example of contagion: how a single default can freeze funding for hundreds of healthy firms, and why regulators watch short-term borrowing so closely.

children.text: The last three lessons covered a global crisis, a currency crisis and a cash crisis. This one is a credit crisis, and it happened almost entirely inside India. It also shows the limits of a central bank: the RBI could ease funding conditions, but it would not simply rescue every non-bank lender.
What NBFCs Do, and Why They Are Fragile

markDefs.definition: A company that lends money but does not hold a banking licence, so it cannot take ordinary deposits from the public and has no direct access to the RBI as a lender of last resort.

children.text: A
non-banking financial company (NBFC)

lends like a bank but cannot take regular deposits. Instead it borrows from banks, mutual funds and bond investors, then lends onward for vehicles, homes, small businesses and infrastructure. NBFCs reach borrowers banks often miss, which makes them important to India, and structurally fragile.

markDefs.definition: Funding long-term loans with short-term borrowing. It is profitable while lenders keep rolling over the short-term debt, and dangerous the moment they refuse.
Short-term unsecured debt, often of 30 to 90 days, issued by companies and bought largely by mutual funds and banks.

children.text: The fragility comes from an
asset-liability mismatch
: many NBFCs funded loans lasting years by issuing
commercial paper
that had to be repaid in weeks. That works only as long as lenders keep rolling the paper over.

body.title: Banks vs NBFCs in a Panic

columns.label: A bank
points: Funded largely by sticky retail deposits
Deposits insured up to ₹5 lakh by DICGC
Can borrow from the RBI through repo and MSF
The RBI can act as lender of last resort

columns.label: An NBFC
points: Funded by commercial paper, bonds and bank loans
No deposit insurance for its lenders
No direct access to RBI liquidity windows
Depends entirely on markets being willing to lend

children.text: How IL&FS Fell Apart

Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services was not a household name, but it was huge and considered rock solid. It funded roads, tunnels and power projects, was part-owned by large institutions including LIC, and carried a group debt of about ₹91,091 crore.

body.title: From AAA to Default in Three Months

events.title: First cracks
events.description: An IL&FS group company defaults on commercial paper and inter-corporate deposits worth about ₹450 crore.

events.title: Chairman resigns
events.description: Ravi Parthasarathy steps down after three decades at the group.

events.title: Ratings slip
events.description: IL&FS loses its AAA rating, which is cut to AA+, still an investment grade that suggested little danger.

events.title: The default that mattered
events.description: IL&FS defaults on a ₹1,000 crore short-term loan from SIDBI, then on bank loans, deposits and commercial paper. Rating agencies downgrade it in huge steps, from investment grade to D, the default grade, within days.

events.title: Panic hits the market
events.description: Fear that other NBFCs face the same funding squeeze triggers a crash in their shares.

events.title: Government takes over
events.description: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs moves the NCLT to supersede the IL&FS board, and a new board chaired by Uday Kotak takes charge of the resolution.

body.text: IL&FS carried the top AAA rating until August 2018, weeks before it defaulted. SEBI later penalised ICRA, CARE and India Ratings ₹1 crore each for lapses in rating its debentures. The lesson for investors: a credit rating is an opinion, updated with a lag, not a guarantee.

children.text: The Day the Market Panicked

On 21 September 2018, a mutual fund sold commercial paper issued by housing financier DHFL at a much higher yield than expected. Markets read that as a sign of distress, and concluded that if lenders would not fund DHFL, they might not fund any NBFC.

stats.label: DHFL intraday fall
stats.context: From a previous close near ₹610 to a low of ₹246.25

stats.label: Sensex intraday swing
stats.context: It fell over 1,100 points before recovering most of it

stats.label: Yes Bank close
stats.context: A separate shock: the RBI had cut short its chief executive's term

body.title: Size Up the DHFL Crash
body.prompt: DHFL fell 364 points to an intraday low of ₹246.25 on 21 September 2018. What was the percentage fall from the previous close? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Previous close = ₹246.25 + ₹364 = about ₹610.25. Fall = −364 ÷ 610.25 × 100 = about -59.6%. Nothing had been announced by DHFL itself that morning. The trigger was one trade in the commercial paper market, which tells you how quickly a funding scare becomes an equity crash.

body.title: Why Did One Default Hurt Every NBFC?
body.question: IL&FS was an infrastructure lender. Why did its default cause a funding squeeze for unrelated NBFCs lending for homes and vehicles?
options: All NBFCs had lent money to IL&FS
Mutual funds and banks that funded NBFCs through short-term paper became afraid of the whole sector, so they stopped rolling over that funding
The RBI ordered banks to stop lending to NBFCs
NBFC borrowers stopped repaying their loans
body.explanation: This is contagion through funding, not through direct exposure. Debt mutual funds and banks were large buyers of NBFC commercial paper. After IL&FS, they worried that any NBFC could be hiding similar problems, so they refused to roll over short-term paper or demanded much higher yields. Even well-run NBFCs suddenly faced a cash crunch.

body.title: What Does a Funding Squeeze Cost?
body.prompt: An NBFC rolls over ₹500 crore of commercial paper every three months. Before the crisis it paid 8% a year; afterwards lenders demand 10%. How much extra interest does it pay over a full year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹500 crore × (10% − 8%) = ₹10 crore a year of extra interest. For a lender earning a thin margin between borrowing and lending rates, a 2 percentage point jump in funding costs can wipe out profitability. Worse, some NBFCs could not borrow at any price, which forced them to stop new lending altogether.

children.text: How the RBI Responded

The RBI faced a hard question: should it act as lender of last resort to institutions it does not guarantee, and which cannot borrow from it directly? Its answer was to ease conditions for banks to fund NBFCs, rather than open a dedicated window for NBFCs themselves.

cells: Bought government bonds to inject durable liquidity: about ₹36,000 crore in October, then ₹40,000 crore each in November and December 2018
Let banks count government securities matching their fresh lending to NBFCs and housing finance companies towards their liquidity requirements, up to 0.5% of NDTL
Raised the single-borrower exposure limit for non-infrastructure NBFCs from 10% to 15% of a bank's capital, until end-2018
Despite reports that the government wanted one, the RBI did not open a dedicated liquidity facility for NBFCs in 2018

body.title: How Much Liquidity Did the OMOs Inject?
body.prompt: The RBI bought about ₹36,000 crore of government bonds in October 2018, ₹40,000 crore in November and ₹40,000 crore in December. What was the total, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹36,000 crore + ₹40,000 crore + ₹40,000 crore = ₹1,16,000 crore, or about ₹1.16 lakh crore in three months. Compare that with the RBI buying a record ₹6.39 lakh crore in FY26, and you can see how much larger its liquidity operations have become.

body.text: This episode overlapped with the public disagreement between the RBI and the government that you read about in Chapter 1, which ended with Governor Urjit Patel resigning in December 2018. How far the RBI should go to support non-banks was one of the issues at the heart of it.

children.text: The Long Tail

The crunch did not end in 2018. Funding stayed expensive and selective for years, and more failures followed. DHFL itself defaulted in 2019 and was eventually taken through insolvency. Weak NBFCs shrank or were bought; strong ones, especially those backed by banks or large groups, gained market share.
Regulators rewrote the rulebook in response.
Liquidity Risk Management Framework, November 2019.
Larger NBFCs must maintain a Liquidity Coverage Ratio, holding enough high quality liquid assets to survive 30 days of stress, phased in to 100% by December 2024.
Scale-Based Regulation, announced October 2021.
NBFCs are sorted into base, middle, upper and top layers, with tighter rules as they grow. The framework took effect from 1 October 2022.
Sharper market discipline.
Debt mutual funds became far more cautious about concentrated exposure to single issuers, and rating agencies faced penalties and closer scrutiny.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why Not Just Rescue Every NBFC?

children.text: A central bank that promises to rescue any institution in trouble creates moral hazard: lenders stop checking whether a borrower is sound, because they assume someone else will pay. That is why the classic rule you met in the 2008 lesson says to lend against good collateral at a penalty rate, and only to institutions that are solvent.

NBFCs sit outside the deposit-insurance and RBI-liquidity safety net precisely because they are not banks. The RBI approach in 2018 reflected that boundary: make it easier and more attractive for banks to lend to sound NBFCs, but do not guarantee the sector. The cost of that choice was a long, grinding funding squeeze. The benefit was that weak lenders were forced to shrink or exit rather than being propped up.

body.title: Your Debt Fund Holds NBFC Paper
body.scenario: It is October 2018. You hold ₹3 lakh in a low duration debt fund. Its latest factsheet shows about 25% of the portfolio in commercial paper and bonds issued by NBFCs and housing finance companies, including a name that has been in the news. Friends are redeeming their debt funds. Your fund has not fallen much, but headlines warn of an NBFC crisis.
body.prompt: How would you assess the risk, and what would you do?
body.modelAnswer: Start by looking at what the fund actually owns rather than the headlines. Open the factsheet and check three things: how concentrated the NBFC exposure is in any single issuer, the credit ratings of those holdings, and the portfolio maturity, since short maturity means papers repay soon and are easier to roll off. The real risk in a debt fund is not day-to-day volatility but credit risk, a default that permanently cuts the NAV, and liquidity risk, where heavy redemptions force the fund to sell into a frozen market. That second risk is what later forced Franklin Templeton to wind up six debt schemes in April 2020. If your fund holds a diversified set of highly rated, short-dated paper, panic redemption is usually the wrong move, because you crystallise a loss and pay exit costs. If it holds a large slice of one stressed issuer, or lower-rated paper for extra yield, reducing exposure is reasonable. The durable lesson: in debt funds, yield above the market average is usually payment for credit risk you may not have noticed.

cards.definition: A lender without a banking licence, funded by markets and banks rather than by public deposits.
Funding long-term loans with short-term borrowing, safe only while lenders keep rolling it over.
Short-term unsecured corporate debt, typically 30 to 90 days, widely bought by debt mutual funds.
When trouble at one institution causes lenders to withdraw funding from similar institutions.
The risk that guaranteed rescues make lenders careless about credit quality.
Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio: government securities banks may count towards liquidity rules, relaxed in 2018 to encourage NBFC lending.
The RBI framework from October 2021 sorting NBFCs into four layers with tighter rules as they grow.

body.label: Screener.in: Check an NBFC Balance Sheet
body.description: Look up any listed NBFC and compare its borrowings, borrowing mix and interest costs across FY18 to FY21 to see how the funding squeeze hit different lenders.

body.title: Assess Credit Risk Like a Professional
steps: Open the latest factsheet of any debt fund you own and list its top five issuers
Check how much of the portfolio sits in a single company or group
Note the share of the portfolio rated below the highest grade
Look up one NBFC you have borrowed from or invested in, and check its mix of short-term versus long-term borrowing
Compare the yield of a fund promising higher returns with a government bond fund, and ask what risk explains the gap

points: NBFCs lend like banks but fund themselves in markets, with no deposit insurance and no direct access to RBI liquidity.
IL&FS, rated AAA until August 2018 with group debt around ₹91,091 crore, defaulted in September 2018 and was downgraded to default grade within days.
The panic spread through funding, not direct exposure: lenders refused to roll over NBFC commercial paper, and DHFL fell about 60% intraday on 21 September 2018.
The RBI eased conditions for banks to lend to NBFCs and injected about ₹1.16 lakh crore through OMOs in late 2018, but did not open a dedicated NBFC window.
The government superseded the IL&FS board on 1 October 2018, installing a new board under Uday Kotak.
The crisis reshaped regulation: liquidity coverage rules for large NBFCs from 2019 and scale-based regulation from 2021.
